analysis.one_liner: Requires phone, cable, satellite, and internet companies to automatically credit customers' bills when service is out.
analysis.headline: The bill has not moved since May 2026: it was read twice in the Senate and referred to the Commerce Committee, with no cosponsors and no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: When your cable, internet, phone, or satellite service goes down for four hours or more, this bill would require the company to automatically credit your bill — one-thirtieth of the monthly rate for each day of outage — without you having to call and ask. Customers who cancel would get leftover credits back as a check, card, or transfer within 30 days. It would also direct the FCC and FTC to write rules on customer service: recordings of support calls available on request, no fee to talk to a representative, standards for missed appointment visits, and easier equipment returns for people with disabilities or without a car [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Residential customers of large telephone, cable, satellite, and internet providers — essentially anyone who pays a monthly bill of $40 or more — gain automatic bill credits for outages of four hours or more, without having to call and negotiate. People with disabilities and people who don't drive would get extra help with equipment returns, and everyone gets a right to recordings of their own customer service calls.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with cable, phone, or internet service

how_it_helps.text: For cable, satellite, internet, and telephone outages lasting 4 hours or more, the bill requires an automatic credit of 1/30 of the monthly rate per day of outage, with no need for the customer to ask [S2].
Customers who cancel service would get any credit balance back within 30 days, by check, no-fee prepaid card, or electronic transfer [S2].

The FCC would write rules extending cable-style customer service standards to satellite, voice, and broadband, requiring call recordings kept for a year and given to customers on request, and barring fees just to reach a live representative [S2].

The FTC would set standards for missed service appointments and, for people with disabilities or who don't drive, require free alternate equipment-return options where returning it is too burdensome [S2].
Broadband providers would have to report outages to the FCC during federally activated disaster areas, so the public record shows where service failed [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large telecom companies (those with more than 5,000 customers) bear the cost: they must credit customer bills during outages, refund departing customers in cash rather than credit, record and retain customer service calls, and comply with new FCC and FTC customer service rules. Providers are exempt from refund requirements when the refund would cost more to deliver than it is worth, which softens the impact on their smallest credits.

drawbacks.text: The refund exception lets providers skip refunds when the amount owed a customer is smaller than the cost of sending it, so the smallest outage credits could go unpaid [S2].
Customers must still notice the outage; the bill credits bills automatically but gives no new avenue to dispute whether an outage lasted the required 4 hours [S2].
Providers could raise prices or reduce service investment to absorb refund costs, and customers would share in any such pass-through; the bill text does not address this [S1].
The bill has no cosponsors and sits in committee, so its promised benefits depend entirely on whether it ever advances — which has not happened [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real but modest: automatic outage credits and refunds end the hassle of calling to request them, and the customer-service rules (call recordings, no fee for a live representative, help for people who can't return equipment) target widely reported frustrations. The main costs fall on large telecom and cable companies, which would absorb credit costs and compliance work; small companies under 5,000 customers are exempt. The bill is narrow and well-scoped, though some technical provisions (what counts as a day of outage) would be worked out in FCC rules. The larger drawback at this point is procedural: it has sat without cosponsors or committee action, so its benefits are theoretical unless it advances.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has not acted on it, and it has attracted no cosponsors.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 18, 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S4] [S1].
No further action has been taken: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no other chamber action is recorded [S1] [S4].
No senator has signed on as a cosponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable, internet, and phone companies are better off so far, since automatic outage credits remain optional and customers must still chase refunds themselves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Telecom and cable companies, for now

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where he is a member.

for.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over communications
for.what_they_did: Holds the bill; has taken no action on it since referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator, a Democrat, is attached to the bill; no votes have occurred, so the partisan shape of support is unknown.

industries.industry: Cable, satellite TV, broadband, and telephone providers (companies with more than 5,000 customers)
industries.note: These companies would owe automatic outage credits and face new FCC and FTC customer-service rules, including call recordings, no fee for a live representative, and easier equipment returns. Consumers who already lose service would stop subsidizing outages with full-price bills. Companies under 5,000 customers are exempt [S2].

analysis.trajectory: First-year bills referred to committee with no cosponsors rarely reach the floor; unless the Commerce Committee schedules a markup or other senators sign on, this bill will most likely die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
